questions.q: Why does the lesson give Claude a second tool (get_exchange_rate) rather than hardcoding the app to always call the API right after the SQL query?
options: Hardcoding the sequence is faster to run
Letting Claude orchestrate across both tools across turns means the API is only called when the question actually needs it, following the multi-tool agent pattern
The Messages API does not allow more than one tool
Hardcoded sequences are not supported by any database driver
questions.explain: Giving Claude both tools lets it decide, based on the actual question and SQL result, whether and when the second tool is needed -- the same multi-tool orchestration pattern from the AI Agents course.

questions.q: In the get_exchange_rate implementation, what does the loop with time.sleep(2 ** attempt) specifically handle?
options: SQL injection attempts
A 429 rate-limit response, by backing off and retrying instead of failing immediately
Invalid currency codes
Database connection timeouts
questions.explain: The exponential backoff loop retries after a 429 (rate-limited) response, giving the API time to recover instead of immediately raising an error.

questions.q: What does resp.raise_for_status() add on top of the timeout and retry logic?
options: It automatically retries forever until success
It raises an exception for any non-success HTTP status, so a bad response doesn't silently get treated as valid data
It converts the response to a different currency
It disables the timeout
questions.explain: raise_for_status() turns an HTTP error response into a Python exception, preventing the code from silently treating a failed request's body as a usable rate.

questions.q: A SQL result has 50 rows but only 4 distinct currency codes. What does this lesson call the mistake of looking up the exchange rate once per row instead of once per distinct currency?
options: The N+1 problem
SQL injection
Schema drift
Tool consolidation
questions.explain: Calling an external dependency once per row instead of deduplicating, caching, or batching across shared values is the N+1 problem, the same pattern that shows up with database queries.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what question specifically requires both a SQL aggregate and a live API call?
options: "List all customers in the orders table"
"What's this month's total revenue in euros?" -- a SQL aggregate for the revenue, plus a live rate to convert it
"What is the capital of France?"
"Show me the most recent order"
questions.explain: That example needs a SQL-computed total and a live, up-to-date exchange rate -- neither source alone can answer it, which is exactly why enrichment matters.
